stories.title: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
stories.summary: The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Figure caption, What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections By James FitzGerald Â and Â Kayla Epstein Published 1 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says. The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, raised a number of questions, including what went wrong? And what happens next? A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who has halted executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. How did it go wrong? Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the 11th hour. Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital, but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring. stories.article_text_excerpt: Russia's Supreme Court is preparing legislation that would allow presiding judges to enter the deliberation room while a jury discusses its verdict and would reduce jury panels from six or eight members to four — changes that could greatly consolidate decision-making power in the hands of state-appointed officials.Deputy Chair of the Supreme Court Nikolai Timoshin and Supreme Court judge Sergei Zelenin have outlined the main provisions of the planned reform, although the draft law has not yet been published.Under the proposals, the presiding judge would not be permitted to vote on a defendant's guilt but would be entitled to "clarify" questions arising during deliberations.Additional provisions would change the procedure for selecting jurors, allow citizens over 65 to serve, restrict the grounds for dissolving an already formed panel and give defendants the right to refuse a jury trial even after a hearing has been scheduled.Jury trials are rare in Russia but produce acquittals at a rate sharply above the national average. stories.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
stories.summary: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NHTI From now on, the US president wants AI to be referred to as 'Super Intelligence' Image: Imaginechina-Tuchong/IMAGO Advertisement What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI). Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives. In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
